bib.title: AgentSkiller: Scaling Generalist Agent Intelligence through Semantically Integrated Cross-Domain Data Synthesis

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AgentSkiller: Scaling Generalist Agent Intelligence through Semantically Integrated Cross-Domain Data Synthesis" (AgentSkiller Technical Report). First author Zexu Sun (equal contribution with Bokai Ji); Baidu AMU, Xidian, SMU, Renmin. Preprint, arXiv:2602.09372v1 [cs.CL], 10 Feb 2026 (p.1). No venue. Code and data are on GitHub and HuggingFace under "AgentSkiller".
COVERAGE: Whole PDF text extracted, 33 pages, 110,496 chars. I read the abstract, method (3.1-3.19), stats (4), experiments (5), conclusion and the appendix start. The appendix prompts (about lines 1727-end) and the references were skimmed or grepped only. Figure text was read as extracted, with no figure images viewed.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Trajectories are synthesized in an 18-step LangGraph DAG pipeline. A text LLM (GPT-5.2) does semantic work. A coding LLM (Claude Opus) writes SQL, MCP servers and unit tests. A "Block Editor" patches failing code, up to K=5 times.
 number: n=15 seed domains expanded to N=300; K=5
 quote: "A Textual LLM (e.g., GPT-5.2) handles high-level semantic reasoning ... while a specialized Coding LLM (e.g., Claude Opus) is dedicated to syntactic precision" and "(default K = 5)"
 where: p.4; p.6 (n=15, N=300); K=5 at about line 795
2. Verification of tasks happens at three levels. (a) Unit tests on each MCP server. (b) Execution-based filtering: the gold tool path is actually run on the MCP server against the grounded database, with failures sorted into policy violation, invalid entity data or server bug. (c) A rollout evaluator that is all-or-nothing. It is the product of binary action, environment and LLM-judge scores. Environment success means the golden DB diff is a subset of the agent's DB diff. Read-only gold calls that are redundant are pruned. Cross-domain tasks skip the filter step because they are validated at creation, with DB backup, rollback and Block Editor repair.
 quote: "S_final = Π s_i, where s_i ∈ {0.0, 1.0}"; "Δgold ⊆ Δagent"
 where: pp.17-20
3. Headline: AgentSkiller-14B is Qwen3-14B after SFT on about 11K trajectories. Setup: SFT only, using verl, 128k sequence length, lr 1e-5, warmup 0.1, cosine schedule. Qwen3-4B/8B/14B were trained. tau-bench and tau2-bench use GPT-5.2 as the user simulator. Results are from Table 1.
 number: tau2-bench overall 79.1 (Retail 77.2, Airline 56.0, Telecom 91.2); tau-bench overall 67.2; ACEBench-Agent 78.0
 quote: "On the complex τ2-bench ... AgentSkiller-14B achieves an overall score of 79.1%, significantly outperforming GPT-o3 with 68.4% and Claude-Sonnet-4 at 56.8%." Also "on ACEBench-Agent, AgentSkiller-14B records a score of 78.0% ... outperforming Gemini-2.5-pro by a margin of 14.6%."
 where: p.23
 Table 1 (p.24) context: GPT-5-think gets 84.2 on tau2 and 67.8 on tau-bench, so it still beats the 14B model. Kimi-K2-1T gets 66.1 on tau2. The 14B is baseline Qwen3-14B +43.0 on tau2 (36.1 to 79.1). Competing data-synthesis baselines at 14B are EnvScaler 42.3, MUA 53.6, ToolMind 47.5 and ToolACE 31.6 on tau2; AgentScaler-30B-A3B gets 62.3.
4. Small students beat much larger models. AgentSkiller-4B gets 66.0 on tau2 versus xLAM-2-70B at 41.0 and Qwen3-Thinking-235B at 58.6. The 8B gets 60.2, and Telecom rises 76.6 to 91.2 from 4B to 14B. The paper reads this as data quality beating parameter count. That is an interpretation. The comparison does not control for training recipe, since the baselines are third-party checkpoints or retrained SFT.
 quote: "AgentSkiller-4B ... achieves an overall τ2-bench score of 66.0%, remarkably outperforming the significantly larger xLAM-2-70B-fc-r at 41.0% and Qwen3-Thinking-235B scoring 58.6%."
 where: p.23
5. The only ablation of the data pipeline is single-domain (SD) subset versus full set (SD plus cross-domain). Model is 14B. tau2 goes 71.2 to 79.1, Retail 69.3 to 77.2, tau-bench 45.4 to 67.2. ACEBench-Agent is unchanged at 78.0. At 4B, ACEBench-Agent drops from 64.0 (SD) to 54.0 (full), and at 8B tau2 and tau-bench move 53.6 to 60.2 and 47.2 to 52.1. Telecom is actually higher for SD at 14B (85.1 vs 91.2 full, so lower). The SD 14B Airline score is 28.0 against 54.0 full.
 quote: "its performance on the more intricate τ2-bench is limited to 71.2%. The integration of cross-domain data in the Full configuration elevates this score to 79.1%"
 where: p.23
 No ablation covers the verification filter, the persona simulator, the policy generation or the unit tests. The paper does not compare filtered against unfiltered data.
6. Data statistics. AgentSkiller-11K is 5,941 single-domain plus 5,581 cross-domain samples. Rollout quality control: of a 13,649-sample pool, the LLM-judge score distribution is 1 to 5, with 314, 1,710, 5,429, 4,932 and 1,264 samples. Excluded samples carry 9,120 issues, led by S1 confirmation omission at 30.5% and R4 unnecessary tool calls at 22.4%.
 quote: "4,299 samples (approximately 31.5% of the total pool) were excluded for failing to meet the 'All-or-Nothing' criteria"
 where: p.21
 The counts do not agree with each other. The text says about 11,522 samples. Section 4.1 says the cross-domain subset is N=11,763 against 5,941 single-domain. Figure 6(b) shows 1,887 excluded samples out of 6,906 plus 6,773. 4,299 excluded out of 13,649 is 31.5%, but 13,649 minus 4,299 is 9,350, not 11.5K. Treat the counts as unreliable.
7. Task and rollout design. Tasks come from enumerating simple paths in a tool graph (NetworkX), between Lmin and Lmax. Gold tasks are grounded to DB rows by constraint-aware sampling (single-domain) or creation-plus-validation (cross-domain). A persona simulator writes a vague "single immediate pain point" startup query with hidden user knowledge (information hiding), which forces the agent to ask clarifying questions. Rollouts are LLM agent against LLM user simulator against mock MCP servers. A fast path caches execution scripts by hash to cut tokens.
 where: pp.15-19
8. Depth analysis on tau2-bench for the 14B. Accuracy against number of tool calls shows Pearson rho of -0.688 (p=0.019) for Retail and -0.566 (p=0.018) for Airline, and +0.300 (p=0.370, not significant) for Telecom. Pass^k is reported only vs AgentScaler-30B-A3B and Qwen3-Thinking-30B-A3B (Fig 7).
 where: p.25

LIMITS
- There is no limitations section. The paper never concedes limitations.
- No contamination or decontamination check against tau-bench, tau2-bench or ACEBench. tau-bench-style retail, airline and telecom domains are not stated to be excluded from the 300 synthesized domains. The synthetic data and the benchmarks share the same form.
- No seeds, no repeated runs, no confidence intervals. There is a single score per cell. Airline-style subsets have small n, so differences of a few points are likely noise.
- BFCL is only cited. It is not evaluated. The benchmarks are tau-bench, tau2-bench and ACEBench-Agent.
- SFT only. No RL, despite the "POMDP / reward" framing in Section 2. The dataset is not used as an RL environment in the experiments.
- The rollout agent model (the one that generates the trajectories) is not named in the pages I read. It is described only as "a target Agent". The text LLM and coding LLM are named: GPT-5.2 and Claude Opus. That means teacher strength and distillation are unquantified.
- Baselines are inconsistent. Several are retrained with SFT on Qwen3 (EnvScaler, MUA, ToolACE). Others are released checkpoints. ACEBench-Agent results for the baselines are unstable (ToolACE 4B gets 26.0, for example).
- GPT-5-think still beats the 14B on tau2 (84.2) and on tau-bench (67.8). The "parity with proprietary" claim is selective. The 4B ACEBench drop with cross-domain data is not explained.
- Claims about "scaling laws" rest on three sizes of one family.

BUILDS ON: APIGen (Liu et al., 2024b) and APIGen-MT (Prabhakar et al., 2025), the forward simulated agent-human interplay paradigm; MAGNET (Yin et al., 2025), the reverse paradigm; AgentScaler (Fang et al., 2025); ToolMind (Yang et al., 2025b); EnvScaler (Song et al., 2026); MUA-RL (Zhao et al., 2025); ToolACE (Liu et al., 2024a); evaluation on tau-bench (Yao et al., 2024), tau2-bench (Barres et al., 2025) and ACEBench (Chen et al., 2025); verl (Sheng et al., 2025); POMDP (Cassandra, 1998).

CODE: none worth keeping. The appendix holds long pipeline prompts, for example a tool-graph prompt with rules like "Single Source of Truth: the node 'Authorize' must be the ONLY node with an..." and "Acyclicity". See the appendix pages, past about p.28.

FIGURES
- Fig 2 (p.5): end-to-end single-domain pipeline, including the golden-trajectory execution and the action, environment and judge evaluators. This is the fastest way to see the verification loop.
- Fig 1 (p.1): bar charts of the three benchmarks, for headline comparison.
- Fig 6 (p.22): score distribution and error taxonomy of excluded samples.
- Fig 8 (p.25): accuracy against tool-call count.
- Fig 9 (appendix): tool-graph examples.

PROBLEMS: A fontTools warning appeared and some figure text came out garbled. No embedded instructions found. The appendix prompts were only skimmed, not read in full. The Table 1 bold and underline marks are lost in the extraction (for example "64.854.0" merges adjacent cells). The sample counts conflict as described in claim 6.

Three verbatim quotes for the note: (1) p.23: "AgentSkiller-14B achieves an overall score of 79.1%, significantly outperforming GPT-o3 with 68.4% and Claude-Sonnet-4 at 56.8%." (2) p.21: "4,299 samples (approximately 31.5% of the total pool) were excluded for failing to meet the 'All-or-Nothing' criteria." (3) p.19: "a failure in any single dimension—whether it be a missed tool call, a database consistency error, or a hallucination—results in a global failure for the task."
